name: Self-heal
habitat: Short grass everywhere — lawns, meadows, path edges, woodland clearings. It survives mowing by flowering low.
identify: SQUARE stem — roll it between your fingers and you can feel the four edges. It is a mint-family plant.
Leaves in opposite pairs, oval, on short stalks.
A dense, blunt, oblong flower head at the stem tip with hooded violet-blue two-lipped flowers emerging from brownish bracts.
Low-growing, often only 10-20 cm in mown grass.
No smell of mint despite the family.

lookalikes.name: Bugle
lookalikes.danger: Low — also a harmless mint-family plant.
lookalikes.tell: Bugle's flowers are spaced in whorls up a leafy spike rather than packed into one blunt terminal head, and it spreads by obvious runners.

lookalikes.name: Ground ivy
lookalikes.tell: Ground ivy has scalloped kidney-shaped leaves and a strong aromatic smell when crushed; self-heal's leaves are plain ovals and it barely smells.

preparations.method: Crush the fresh plant and press onto the wound.
preparations.for_use: The name is the traditional use — a styptic and wound herb for shallow cuts and grazes.

preparations.method: Steep the dried aerial parts 10 minutes.
preparations.for_use: A gargle for sore throat and mouth ulcers, and a wound wash.

cautions: Taken from lawns, so the contamination question matters more than the plant does — avoid sprayed or dog-walked ground.
Mildly anticoagulant activity is reported; caution alongside blood thinners.
A minor styptic. Direct pressure remains the answer for real bleeding.
evidence: Widespread traditional use in both European and Chinese medicine; laboratory antiviral and antibacterial activity is reported. Clinical evidence is thin.
